title: What If Every Bank Closed for Six Months? Ireland's Did in 1970

scenes.text: What if a country's banks closed for six months? In 1970, Ireland found out.
On May 1st, bank staff went on strike, and the country's main banks stayed shut until November 17th.
No deposits, no withdrawals, nothing cleared. So people kept writing cheques, and passed them on like cash.
But who could you trust? The answer was the pub. Ireland had about 11,000 of them, and a publican knew who was good for it.
Pubs and shops vouched for their regulars, and a country of three million people ran on IOUs.
When the banks reopened, a mountain of cheques was waiting. The economy hadn't collapsed. It had kept growing.

description:
What if a country's banks shut their doors for half a year?
It happened in Ireland. A strike closed the main clearing banks from 1 May to 17 November 1970, six and a half months. People could not deposit, withdraw or clear anything, so they kept writing cheques and passed them from hand to hand as a kind of private money, trusting that they would be honoured when the banks came back. Deciding whose cheque was good fell largely to the country's roughly 11,000 pubs and 12,000 shops, whose owners knew their customers well. When the banks reopened, millions of cheques worth billions of pounds were waiting to be cleared, and normal business did not return until early 1971. Studies, including one by the economist Antoin Murphy in 1978, found the economy kept growing and retail sales held up, although the episode was not painless.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Some people reportedly wrote cheques on whatever paper was at hand. Who would vouch for you if the banks shut tomorrow?
